In the early 1970s, towards the end of the Vietnam War, a castle in the Pacific Northwest is used by the US government as an insane asylum for military personnel.

Among the patients is former astronaut Billy Cutshaw, who aborted a Moon launch and was dragged screaming from the capsule, suffering from an apparent mental breakdown. Colonel Hudson Kane, a former member of a USMC special unit, arrives at the castle to take over the treatment of the patients.

Once you see The Ninth Configuration as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. Lieutenant Reno, who is there attempting to stage Shakespeare plays with a cast of dogs, suspects that Kane is crazy himself. Meanwhile, Kane constantly has nightmares of his brother Vincent, a former patient and murderer who is now dead.

The story The Ninth Configuration tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. Cutshaw talks with Kane again, and they debate God and the idea of a divine plan. Kane, who believes that the existence of a God is far more likely than humanity's having emerged from "random chance", argues that deeds of pure self-sacrifice are proof of human goodness, which can only be explained by divine purpose.

Meaning is not found in The Ninth Configuration — it is manufactured for it. Cutshaw demands that Kane recall one concrete example of pure self-sacrifice from his personal experience; Kane is unable. Kane takes Cutshaw to a church service, which Cutshaw interrupts with several outbursts, and Kane momentarily hallucinates.
